142.history: The inland seat of the Tuathaich keeps its own book of its elders. The black cake of the north was sold at its market by the basket beside the peat from the second year. Word of the pit towns' agreement reached its elders by a carrier in the sixteenth year, and they sent nothing west and nothing to Tional nan Tuathach. In the war its people sent three carts of meal to the western families at Doire ghlas and asked no receipt. In the year of the passes the northern office set a clerk in its old wool-hall, and the elders had their own names written first; in the present year they show their passes at An siathamh rèisimeid's posts going south to the fair, and write in their book that the sergeant wished them a good road. Cnoc ghorm has never had a pit or a light or a regiment; it is a town of the Tuathaich markets and councils and it sends its delegates to Tional nan Tuathach.
142.known_for: the inland seat of the Tuathaich and its elders' book

248.history: The small western crossing lay on the column's road. Its report in {{year:VI-0112}} is the first An Clàr Foscailte copies: the smith's boy woke the maor, Cailean mac Griogair, who stood at the field's edge in a borrowed coat and watched the column ford the water without going down to ask where it was bound, and the miller's wife, watching from the mill loft, saw no banner among them and no drum, only a man at the head whom the rest left the whole width of the road. It is a village of a mill, a smithy and a score of houses beside the ford, and its people had never, before that night, sent a report to the Board of anything. Its maor's report and the miller's wife's words stand together in the library's file, the first two papers of the column's road.

360.history: The small mill town on Rathad na Fèille a day's walk from the capital gave its name to both the old battle and the last of An Cogadh Fada. The column camped on its fields in {{year:VI-0113}}, and the first and third regiments came down Rathad na Fèille to meet it. In the morning's fighting the mill was taken by the column and taken back, the miller's wife moving her pots out of whatever corner the fighting last left; An treas rèisimeid's four guns, hauled the last two miles by hand, found the column's thorn-stand line; at dusk sixty came out of the byres unarmed under a white cloth on a byre-fork, and the regiments' surgeon treated both sides alike. The field was sown again in {{year:VI-0127}}, and its farmer hands the weapons his plough turns up to A' chiad rèisimeid, which keeps a list. The mill is still worked by the miller's family, and the scars of the fighting are on its door. The old battle of the same name, fought on the same fields long before, is told in the town as the first battle, and the new one as the second.
360.known_for: Blàr Muileann ghlas, the last battle of An Cogadh Fada
